directAnswer: St. Sixtus I, also written Xystus, was the seventh bishop of Rome in the early second century. Irenaeus lists him sixth after the apostles, and the Liber Pontificalis attributes several liturgical rules to him. Little more is known, and the claim that he died a martyr is unverified.

paras: The original Greek form of his name was Xystus, and Irenaeus places him sixth from the apostles, a position that later writers noted as fitting the name. Eusebius gives him a pontificate of about ten years in the reign of Emperor Hadrian. He is the first of three popes to bear the name in the early Church, followed by the martyr Sixtus II and by Sixtus III in the fifth century.
The Liber Pontificalis describes him as a Roman, son of Pastor, which fits the note that he was of Greek descent but raised in Italy. The details cannot be confirmed.

Later sources credit Sixtus I with decreeing that only sacred ministers should touch the sacred vessels and that the people should join the celebrant in singing the Sanctus at Mass. As with other early popes, historians regard these as customs of later centuries that were assigned to an ancient name.
He is honored as a martyr, but no early account of his death exists. The town of Alatri, southeast of Rome, has long claimed to hold his relics. His traditional feast is April 6.

keyFacts: Seventh bishop of Rome; Greek name Xystus
Placed sixth after the apostles in Irenaeus’s list
Later sources credit him with rules on the sacred vessels and the Sanctus
Relics claimed by the town of Alatri, Italy

faqs.question: Is Pope Sixtus I the same as the St. Sixtus in the Mass?
faqs.answer: No. The Sixtus named in the Roman Canon is Sixtus II, who was beheaded in 258 during the persecution of Valerian. Sixtus I lived more than a century earlier.

faqs.question: What decrees are attributed to Pope Sixtus I?
faqs.answer: The Liber Pontificalis says he reserved the handling of sacred vessels to ministers and had the people sing the Sanctus with the priest. Historians think these attributions reflect later practice rather than his own legislation.
